difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: two directly linked concepts (unit row sums make the all-ones vector an eigenvector with eigenvalue 1; a singular homogeneous system has infinitely many solutions) in 2-3 short steps, about 1.5 min for a prepared student.
stem: The sum of the elements in each row of $A \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ is 1. If $B = A^3 - 2A^2 + A$, which one of the following statements is correct (for $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$)?

options.label: B
options.text: The equation $Bx = 0$ has exactly two solutions

options.label: C
options.text: The equation $Bx = 0$ has infinitely many solutions

options.label: D
options.text: The equation $Bx = 0$ has a unique solution

solution.quick: Unit row sums mean $A\mathbf{1} = \mathbf{1}$ for the all-ones vector $\mathbf{1}$. Then $B\mathbf{1} = A^3\mathbf{1} - 2A^2\mathbf{1} + A\mathbf{1} = \mathbf{1} - 2\cdot\mathbf{1} + \mathbf{1} = \mathbf{0}$. So $B$ has a non-zero null vector and is singular, and $Bx = 0$ has infinitely many solutions (every $c\mathbf{1}$, $c \in \mathbb{R}$). Answer **(C)**.

steps.title: Translate the row-sum condition
steps.body:
Let $\mathbf{1} = (1, 1, \dots, 1)^\top \in \mathbb{R}^n$. The $i$-th entry of $A\mathbf{1}$ is

$$(A\mathbf{1})_i = \sum_{j=1}^{n} a_{ij}\cdot 1 = \text{(sum of row } i) = 1.$$

So $A\mathbf{1} = \mathbf{1}$: the all-ones vector is an eigenvector of $A$ with eigenvalue $1$.

steps.title: Apply $B$ to the all-ones vector
steps.body:
Powers of $A$ keep the same eigenvector: $A^2\mathbf{1} = A(A\mathbf{1}) = A\mathbf{1} = \mathbf{1}$ and $A^3\mathbf{1} = A(A^2\mathbf{1}) = \mathbf{1}$. Hence

$$B\mathbf{1} = A^3\mathbf{1} - 2A^2\mathbf{1} + A\mathbf{1} = \mathbf{1} - 2\,\mathbf{1} + \mathbf{1} = \mathbf{0}.$$

Equivalently, $B = p(A)$ with $p(t) = t^3 - 2t^2 + t = t(t-1)^2$, so $B = A(A-I)^2$. Because $(A - I)\mathbf{1} = \mathbf{0}$ and $p(1) = 1 - 2 + 1 = 0$, the value $0$ is an eigenvalue of $B$ with eigenvector $\mathbf{1}$.

steps.title: Consequence for $Bx = 0$
steps.body:
A homogeneous system always has the trivial solution $x = \mathbf{0}$. Here $\mathbf{1} \ne \mathbf{0}$ is also a solution, and so is every multiple:

$$B(c\mathbf{1}) = c\,B\mathbf{1} = \mathbf{0} \quad \text{for all } c \in \mathbb{R}.$$

So $B$ is singular ($\det B = 0$, $\operatorname{rank} B \le n-1$, nullity $\ge 1$), and $Bx = 0$ has **infinitely many** solutions. This holds for every $A$ with unit row sums and every $n \ge 1$. (If $A = I$, for instance, then $B = I - 2I + I = 0$ and every $x$ is a solution.)

steps.title: Check on a concrete matrix
steps.body:
Take $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$ (row sums $2 - 1 = 1$ and $0 + 1 = 1$). Then

$$A^2 = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \quad A^3 = \begin{bmatrix} 8 & -7 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \quad B = A^3 - 2A^2 + A = \begin{bmatrix} 8 - 8 + 2 & -7 + 6 - 1 \\ 0 & 1 - 2 + 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}.$$

$Bx = 0$ reduces to $2x_1 - 2x_2 = 0$, i.e. $x_1 = x_2$. The solution set is $\{c(1, 1)^\top : c \in \mathbb{R}\}$, which is infinitely many solutions. Note that this $A$ is itself invertible ($\det A = 2$), yet $B$ is singular.

solution.teaching:
**Row sums are a matrix–vector product.** Multiplying a matrix by the all-ones vector adds up each row: $(A\mathbf{1})_i = \sum_j a_{ij}$. So "every row sums to 1" is exactly the statement $A\mathbf{1} = \mathbf{1}$. In other words, $\mathbf{1}$ is an eigenvector of $A$ with eigenvalue $1$. Row-stochastic (Markov transition) matrices are the best-known example, but the entries do not have to be non-negative for this to work.

**Polynomials of a matrix act on eigenvectors through the same polynomial.** If $Av = \lambda v$, then $A^k v = \lambda^k v$ for every $k$, so for any polynomial $p$,

$$p(A)\,v = p(\lambda)\,v.$$

In particular, if $p(\lambda) = 0$, then $p(A)$ sends the non-zero vector $v$ to $\mathbf{0}$, so $p(A)$ is singular.

**Solutions of a homogeneous system.** The solutions of $Bx = 0$ form the null space of $B$, which is a subspace. There are only two possibilities:

- $B$ is invertible ($\det B \ne 0$): the only solution is $x = \mathbf{0}$ (unique).
- $B$ is singular ($\det B = 0$): the null space contains a non-zero vector $v$, and then every $cv$ is a solution, giving infinitely many.

"No solution" is impossible because $x = \mathbf{0}$ always works. "Exactly two solutions" is impossible because solutions come in whole lines through the origin.

**Back to the question.** Here $p(t) = t^3 - 2t^2 + t$ and $\lambda = 1$, so $p(1) = 1 - 2 + 1 = 0$. Therefore $B\mathbf{1} = \mathbf{0}$, $B$ is singular, and $Bx = 0$ has infinitely many solutions: option (C).

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: A homogeneous system $Bx = 0$ always has at least the trivial solution $x = \mathbf{0}$, for any matrix $B$. It can never have no solution.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: The solution set of $Bx = 0$ is a subspace: if $x \ne \mathbf{0}$ is a solution, so is $cx$ for every real $c$. It therefore has either exactly one solution or infinitely many, never exactly two.

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: $A\mathbf{1} = \mathbf{1}$ gives $B\mathbf{1} = \mathbf{1} - 2\cdot\mathbf{1} + \mathbf{1} = \mathbf{0}$ with $\mathbf{1} \ne \mathbf{0}$. So $B$ is singular and every $c\mathbf{1}$ solves $Bx = 0$.

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: A unique solution ($x = \mathbf{0}$ only) would require $B$ to be invertible. But $B\mathbf{1} = \mathbf{0}$ shows that $B$ is singular for every $A$ with unit row sums.

solution.shortcut: Options (A) and (B) are impossible for any homogeneous system, so only (C) and (D) remain. Unit row sums mean eigenvalue $1$ with eigenvector $\mathbf{1}$, and $p(1) = 1 - 2 + 1 = 0$, so $B$ is singular and (C) is the answer.
solution.commonTrap: Choosing (D) on the belief that a homogeneous system has only the trivial solution, or thinking more information about $A$ is needed (e.g. whether $A$ is invertible). $A$ may well be invertible (e.g. $A = I$), but $B = A(A-I)^2$ is always singular because $(A - I)\mathbf{1} = \mathbf{0}$.

answerVerification.independentAnswer: C (A1 = 1 gives B1 = 0, so B is singular and Bx = 0 has infinitely many solutions)
answerVerification.checkCode:
import numpy as np, sympy as sp
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
for n in [1, 2, 3, 5, 8]:
    for trial in range(200):
        A = rng.normal(size=(n, n)); A[:, -1] += 1 - A.sum(axis=1)   # force every row sum = 1 (entries may be negative)
        B = A @ A @ A - 2 * A @ A + A
        one = np.ones(n)
        assert np.allclose(A @ one, one) and np.allclose(B @ one, 0)
        assert np.linalg.matrix_rank(B, tol=1e-8) < n                 # B singular -> nontrivial null space
print('B @ 1 = 0 and rank(B) < n in every trial')
# exact symbolic check for a generic 3x3 matrix with unit row sums
a = sp.symbols('a0:6'); A = sp.Matrix([[a[0], a[1], 1 - a[0] - a[1]], [a[2], a[3], 1 - a[2] - a[3]], [a[4], a[5], 1 - a[4] - a[5]]])
B = A**3 - 2 * A**2 + A
print('symbolic B*1 =', sp.simplify(B * sp.ones(3, 1)).T, ' det(B) =', sp.factor(B.det()))
# worked example from the solution
A = np.array([[2, -1], [0, 1]]); B = A @ A @ A - 2 * A @ A + A
print('example B =', B.tolist(), ' B @ [1,1] =', (B @ np.ones(2)).tolist(), ' rank =', np.linalg.matrix_rank(B))

B is therefore singular and Bx = 0 has infinitely many solutions, i.e. option (C). This matches the official key C. The Python check confirms B1 = 0 and rank(B) < n for 1000 random real matrices with unit row sums (n = 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, entries allowed to be negative). A symbolic 3x3 check gives B1 = 0 and det(B) = 0 identically, and the worked 2x2 example gives B = [[2, -2], [0, 0]].
